title: PISA Cope in the Pages of Tes Magazine
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman argues that the education sector's reaction to England's improved PISA 2025 results reveals a field that lacks working correctives to its own bias. He opens with a general claim that everyone is biased and that the scientific method and open debate exist precisely to check that bias, then contends that many education commentators, including tes editor Jon Severs, are reaching for caveats to explain away results that vindicate the Gove and Gibb reforms. The core of the piece is a close look at the non-response bias analysis, which found that non-participating pupils in England were slightly more likely to be disadvantaged or have SEND. Ashman argues this pattern is almost inherent to a voluntary, low-stakes test that permits SEND exclusions everywhere, and that cross-country comparisons of free school meals or SEND percentages are not meaningful because systems classify pupils differently. He uses Scotland as a counterexample, where the participation gap was similar or larger yet results kept declining. He closes by challenging Christian Bokhove's claim of upward bias in England's sample as unsupportable.
points: Ashman frames the PISA debate as a test of whether education has functioning correctives to bias, suggesting the field's disdain for the scientific method has produced an immune response against inconvenient data.

The non-response analysis showing non-participants were more likely to be FSM-eligible or have SEND is, he argues, an expected feature of any voluntary, low-stakes assessment with permitted SEND exclusions, not a quirk unique to England.
Comparing FSM or SEND percentages across countries is invalid because each system classifies disadvantage and additional needs differently, and Australia has no national FSM equivalent at all.
Scotland shows a similar or larger participation gap on free school meals yet its PISA scores kept falling, which undercuts the claim that sampling explains England's gains.
He reads tes magazine's editorial stance as partly audience capture, praising coverage that foregrounds caveats as 'balanced' while treating positive readings as suspect.
quotes: The danger comes when people do not believe they are biased. If you think one view is balanced or objective, then the need for correctives such as the scientific method and free debate recedes.

When its brightest stars can be so wrong for so long, it suggests education lacks correctives to bias. It is perhaps no coincidence that this is accompanied by such disdain for the scientific method among many in educational academia, or that many of us have experienced attempts to shut down debate. Perhaps educational bias has developed an immune response.

He may have judged that his audience would be delighted to read about the extensive caveats that we should apply to this data—caveats that mostly apply to every country and every round of PISA, but that seem particularly significant to Severs right now.

It identifies schools to take part that appear to be representative, but it knows some will not respond, so it also identifies a reserve list. Moreover, in the schools that take part, it does not force each individual student to participate.
Can I believe that students who do not participate in a non-compulsory, low-stakes assessment will be more likely to be disadvantaged or have additional needs? Absolutely.

But countries cannot be compared directly in this because they all have different ways of classifying additional needs and different systems for responding to disadvantage. Australia, for example, has no national equivalent of England’s free school meals system.
And yet Scotland’s PISA results have continued their relentless decline. This prompted the most deliciously grudging correction from Kemp:
Even when countries have free school meals systems, such as Scotland and England, the comparison is fraught and does not necessarily support the idea that England’s sample is unusual.
